sharedText: in the twenty and sixth year
reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter, on a six-word run, and it is regnal-year dating and nothing else. 1 Kings 16:8 dates the accession of Elah of Israel; 3 Nephi 6:1 dates the return of the Nephites to their lands after the robber war. The Book of Mormon dates every paragraph of this chapter the same way — 6:4 'the twenty and sixth and seventh years', 6:9 'the twenty and eighth year', 6:10 'the twenty and ninth year', 6:14 and 6:17 'the thirtieth year' — so the rarity that made the phrase rank is arithmetic rather than intertextual: the KJV had occasion to write 'twenty and sixth' about a reign once, and this chapter had occasion to write it about a year of the judges once. This entry covers every regnal-dating candidate in the chapter, including Ezekiel 1:1 at 6:14 ('in the thirtieth year') and Revelation 21:1 at 6:4 ('passed away, and there was'), which are the same phenomenon reached through different numerals and different connectives.

“entered into a covenant” occurs in exactly two KJV verses — 2 Chronicles 15:12, Asa's national covenant to seek the LORD, and Ezekiel 16:8, the LORD's marriage covenant with Jerusalem — which is rare enough to be worth checking and not enough to be a source. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase for a treaty with surrendered robbers here and, twenty-five verses later, for the secret oath of the judges: 'they did enter into a covenant one with another, yea, even into that covenant which was given by them of old, which covenant was given and administered by the Devil' (6:28). One chapter using the phrase in both senses, one of them diabolical, is a phrase the book owns, not one it is borrowing. Nothing else of 2 Chronicles 15 is present.

A four-word run and pure homography. In Joshua 4:18 what is lifted up is the soles of the priests' feet, out of the Jordan onto dry land, and the clause is a physical description of the end of a miracle. In 3 Nephi 6:10 what is lifted up is the people, into pride and boastings because of their riches. The verb is not even the same verb in sense — one is elevation of a body, the other is a moral state — and the preposition 'unto' governs a place in Joshua and an abstraction in the Book of Mormon. The real source of the pride language in this verse is discussed at the James 4:16 link and at the 1 Timothy 3:6 entry below.

This one is genuinely tempting and it is being declined on the preposition. “lifted up with pride” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 3:6 — 'Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil' — and the fit with this chapter is uncomfortably good, since 3 Nephi 6:15 says in so many words that 'Satan had great power' over exactly these people, which is Paul's 'condemnation of the devil' arriving five verses later. But the Book of Mormon never once writes 'with'. It writes 'lifted up unto pride' here, 'lifted up in pride' three verses later, and 'lifted up in the pride of their hearts' or 'of their eyes' dozens of times from 2 Nephi onward, in books adjudicated before this one. A formula the corpus has used continuously for four hundred pages, with a preposition the KJV verse does not have, is the corpus's own; the singleton is a coincidence of the two words that surround it. Recorded at length because a reader who runs the rarity check will find the singleton and should be told the catalogue found it too and why it declined.

sharedText: (social rank distinguished by wealth inside a congregation)
reason: The thematic pull is strong and the wording will not bear it. James 2:1-9 is the New Testament's one sustained passage on a church that sorts its members by wealth — the gay clothing and the good place, the poor man under the footstool, 'are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts' — and 3 Nephi 6:12 is a church sorted by wealth into ranks, immediately followed by the church being broken up. The catalogue does link this verse's neighbourhood to James, but through James 4:13-5:6 at 6:10, where three KJV singletons and a preserved sequence carry the case. At 6:12 itself there is not one shared distinctive word: James has respect of persons, apparel, and a synagogue; the Book of Mormon has ranks, riches, learning and poverty. Filed here so that the reading is recorded as considered rather than missed.

A four-word run in opposite senses, and the difference is a matter of English idiom rather than of theology. Matthew 24:43's goodman 'would not have suffered his house to be broken up' — that is, broken into, burgled by the thief who comes in the night; the KJV's 'broken up' there translates the digging through of a mud wall. 3 Nephi 6:14's church 'was broken up in all the land', which is dissolution, a body ceasing to hold together. Nothing else of the Olivet discourse is in the verse, and the eschatological setting that might have made the parallel interesting cuts the wrong way: Matthew's householder fails to watch and loses his goods, while the Nephite church fails and loses itself.

“the hearts of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is the kind of fact that ought to settle a link and here does not. Joshua 7:5's hearts melt and become as water: it is a description of national terror after the defeat at Ai. 3 Nephi 6:16's hearts are led away by Satan into iniquity: it is a description of national seduction. The verb governs the noun in opposite directions — fear that paralyses versus desire that moves — and the two verses share no other word. The near miss is worth naming: Joshua 7 is a story about a man who coveted silver, gold and a goodly garment and brought the whole people down with him, which is almost the argument of 3 Nephi 6:10-16, and a catalogue that recorded the singleton without recording that it is the wrong half of Joshua 7 would be making a false economy.

sharedText: (a conspirator drawing away the hearts of a people to seize a throne)
reason: “stole the hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse: 'so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel', and the narrative it opens is the closest biblical analogue to what 3 Nephi 6 describes — a subversion worked through the judgment-seat (2 Samuel 15:2-4, Absalom promising better justice to every man who came to the king for judgment), ending in a conspiracy to displace the ruler and take the crown, which is 3 Nephi 6:30 exactly. But the Book of Mormon writes 'lead away the hearts of the people', which shares with 2 Samuel 15:6 only the noun 'hearts', and 'lead away' is itself a KJV singleton belonging to an unrelated verse (Isaiah 20:4, the Assyrian deporting Egyptians). Typology without wording, and the Ehud entry at Helaman 1:10 is the model for how the catalogue handles that: record it, decline it, and let the reader see the type was seen.

sharedText: (ignorance as the plea for those who kill the just)
reason: The most interesting thing declined in this chapter. Acts 3:17 is Peter's excuse for the men who had just killed Jesus — 'I wot that through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers' — and it stands behind Luke 23:34's 'they know not what they do'. 3 Nephi 6:18 says of a people who are about to kill their prophets, and who are four chapters from the crucifixion in the other hemisphere, that they 'did not sin ignorantly'. The plea Peter grants Jerusalem is refused to Zarahemla, and the refusal is placed immediately before the killings. That is a real reading and the catalogue believes it, but it is not a verbal dependence: Acts 3:17 has 'through ignorance', a phrase the KJV uses eight times and always in the Levitical law, while 3 Nephi 6:18 has the adverb 'ignorantly', whose Book of Mormon setting is the sacrificial law of Numbers 15:28 and whose paired term 'wilfully' comes from Hebrews 10:26. The link at 6:18 is written there, against Hebrews and Numbers; this entry records the Acts reading and says why it is not the source.

A five-word run and the wrong governor. John 2:8's governor is the ruler of the feast at Cana, the master of ceremonies who tastes the water made wine; the word renders architriklinos and has no judicial content at all. 3 Nephi 6:23's governor is the head of state whose warrant is required before an execution, and whose ignorance of the killings is the point of the verse. The KJV's eight 'governor of the —' phrases are of a city, a house, the country, the Jews and the feast, and none of them is 'the governor of the land', which occurs in no KJV verse. The chapter's real debt on this point is to John 18:31 and is catalogued at 6:22; the coincidence is that both come from John.

sharedText: any man should be put to death
reason: Cross-reference, not a rejection. This is the verse with the closest verbal contact in the chapter — “put any man to death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 18:31's 'It is not lawful for us to put any man to death', and 6:24 reads 'this was contrary to the laws of the land, that any man should be put to death, except they had power from the governor of the land', which is the same rule stated from the other side of the passive. The link is nevertheless catalogued two verses earlier, at 6:22, where the rule is given together with the personnel it binds — lawyer, judge, high priest — because that is where a reader meets the whole of what John 18:31 supplies. A reader arriving at 6:24 is sent there.
